prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MARANA, Arizona (CNN) -- I've been privileged in the past to witness Tiger Woods out on a golf course. And I can tell you, it's a painful, frustrating process. Golf fans flocked to Arizona to see Tiger make his long-awaited return to the tee. Not because the golf he produces isn't spectacular and at times utterly dazzling but it's the sheer volume of people he attracts that help convince me each and every time golf has to be one of the worst "out on the course" spectator sports going. That's just my opinion though. Try telling that to the legions who got themselves to Arizona this week once they heard the world's top player was making his return to the game after more than eight months. Woods' first competitive slice of action in the best part of a year wasn't due to get under way until around lunchtime here though judging by the fans already out on the course you'd have thought his tee-time was more like 7am. Even those jostling for position to catch a glimpse of him on the range or putting green were taking no chances and ensuring they arrived in plenty of time. Remember all of this was before he even teed off! The scene on that first hole was as expected bustling to say the least. The small gantries were packed anyway due to the whole array of talent on show through this week, but it got even more frenzied when the Woods-Jones match- up was announced. Mayhem to say the least! Those seated in the stands were the lucky ones, it was the unfortunate spectators trying to stand and strain every sinew to catch a glance of that first shot from the world number one I felt for. Even us media suffered! With seconds to go before the American struck his drive, one television camera crew, which really should have known better, blatantly blocked us from getting that prized shot. Only quick last-gasp thinking from our cameraman John saved the day. In case you were wondering that Woods drive was just majestic and he would go on to win the first two holes in fine style. When he strode off down the first fairway, there was a stampede with those looking to brave the soaring temperatures here in Arizona and follow him every step of the way. The Woods 'wow factor' is still very much alive and kicking. The question is will the so-called bionic knee hold up in the weeks and months to come?

outputs.L1:
MARANA, Arizona (CNN) -- I’ve had the privilege of watching Tiger Woods on a golf course before, and I can tell you that, for a spectator, it can be a painful and frustrating experience.

That is not because the golf he produces is anything less than spectacular—and, at times, utterly dazzling—but because of the sheer number of people he attracts. Each time, it reinforces my belief that golf must be one of the worst sports to watch from out on the course.

That is just my opinion, of course. Try telling it to the legions of fans who made their way to Arizona this week after learning that the world’s top player would be returning to the game following an absence of more than eight months.

Woods’ first taste of competitive action in the best part of a year was not due to begin until around lunchtime. Yet, judging by the number of fans already on the course, you might have thought his tee time was closer to 7 a.m.

Even those jostling for position to catch a glimpse of him on the driving range or putting green were taking no chances, arriving well in advance. And remember, all of this happened before he had even teed off.

As expected, the scene at the first hole was bustling, to say the least. The small grandstands were already packed because of the array of talent on display throughout the week, but the atmosphere became even more frenzied when the Woods-Jones matchup was announced.

It was mayhem.

Those seated in the stands were the lucky ones. I felt for the less fortunate spectators who were standing and straining every sinew simply to catch a glimpse of the world No. 1’s opening shot.

Even those of us in the media suffered. With only seconds remaining before the American struck his drive, a television camera crew—which really should have known better—blatantly blocked our view of that prized shot. Only some quick, last-gasp thinking by our cameraman, John, saved the day.

In case you were wondering, Woods’ drive was simply majestic, and he went on to win the first two holes in fine style.

As he strode down the first fairway, a stampede followed, with fans prepared to brave Arizona’s soaring temperatures to track his every step.

The Woods “wow factor” is still very much alive and kicking. The question is whether his so-called bionic knee will hold up in the weeks and months ahead.

MARANA, Arizona (CNN) — I’ve had the good fortune to watch Tiger Woods play in person before, and the experience can be both uncomfortable and exasperating. That has nothing to do with the quality of his golf, which is often extraordinary and occasionally breathtaking. Rather, it is the enormous crowd he draws that repeatedly leaves me thinking golf may be among the least spectator-friendly sports to watch from the course itself.

That is only my view, of course, and the countless fans who traveled to Arizona this week would strongly disagree. Once word spread that the world’s top-ranked golfer was returning after an absence of more than eight months, they arrived in force.

Woods was not scheduled to begin his first competitive round in almost a year until around midday. Yet the number of spectators already gathered made it seem as though he were teeing off at 7 a.m. Fans hoping to see him on the practice range or putting green came especially early to secure a good position—and all of this happened before he had even started his round.

Predictably, the first tee was extremely crowded. The small viewing stands were already full because of the impressive field competing during the week, but the announcement of the Woods-Jones pairing pushed the atmosphere into outright chaos.

Those with seats were fortunate. I felt sorry for the spectators standing outside the stands, stretching and struggling simply to glimpse the world number one’s opening shot. Even members of the media had difficulties. Just seconds before Woods hit his drive, a television camera crew—which should have known better—moved directly into our line of sight and nearly ruined our chance to capture the moment. Our cameraman, John, reacted quickly at the last possible second and rescued the shot.

For anyone wondering, Woods’ opening drive was magnificent, and he went on to win the first two holes impressively. As he walked down the first fairway, a wave of spectators rushed after him, prepared to endure Arizona’s rising heat in order to follow his every move.

Tiger’s famous “wow factor” clearly remains intact. The bigger issue is whether his so-called bionic knee will withstand the demands of the coming weeks and months.
outputs.L3:

His comeback generated enormous excitement, with huge crowds arriving hours before his lunchtime tee time. Many hoped to watch him practise, while others were determined to secure the best possible viewing position.

The scene also highlighted how frustrating golf can be as a spectator sport. Woods attracts such vast crowds that visibility is often severely limited, making it difficult for many fans to catch more than a brief glimpse of the action. The first hole became especially chaotic when the Woods-Jones matchup was announced, prompting spectators to surge into position and leaving many struggling to see Woods’ opening shot.

Despite the surrounding mayhem and intense attention, Woods showed little sign of rust. He struck a majestic opening drive and went on to win the first two holes in impressive fashion, providing an emphatic start to his long-awaited return.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person CNN-style sports report from Marana, Arizona, describing the crowds and media frenzy surrounding Tiger Woods’s return to competitive golf after an eight-month absence.
counterfactuals.output:
**MARANA, Arizona (CNN) —** I’m standing along the fairways at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Club, where the atmosphere feels more like a major championship than the opening round of a match-play event.

Tiger Woods is back.

After eight months away from competitive golf following reconstructive knee surgery, the world’s top-ranked player returned Wednesday at the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship—and thousands of spectators surged across the desert course to witness it.

From the moment Woods stepped onto the first tee, fans packed several rows deep behind the ropes. They climbed hillsides, crowded around greens and hurried between holes, trying to catch even a brief glimpse of his swing. Cheers followed nearly every shot, while marshals repeatedly urged the gallery to stand still and make room.

The media presence has been just as intense. Camera crews, photographers and reporters have descended on Marana from around the world, tracking Woods’s every step and searching for signs of how his repaired left knee will respond under tournament pressure.

Woods showed little rust in his opening match against Australia’s Brendan Jones. His drives drew roars across the course, and each successful putt seemed to reassure the crowd that golf’s biggest star had truly returned. Woods won the match 3 and 2, ending it on the 16th hole.

But the score was almost secondary. For much of the day, the real story was the spectacle surrounding him: the moving wall of spectators, the clicking cameras and the palpable sense that professional golf had regained its central figure.

Here in the Arizona desert, Tiger Woods’s comeback is not simply another tournament appearance. It is the event everyone came to see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a lively on-the-scene article about Tiger Woods returning to the course in Arizona, emphasizing how difficult it is for spectators to catch a glimpse of him and questioning whether his surgically repaired knee will hold up.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tiger’s Return Turns Desert Course Into a Moving Stampede**

**MARANA, Ariz.** — First came the roar. Then the forest of raised arms, cameras and sun hats. Somewhere in the middle of it all, barely visible above the shoulders of thousands of spectators, Tiger Woods was walking onto a golf course again.

After eight months away and reconstructive surgery on his left knee, Woods returned at the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship, transforming a quiet stretch of Arizona desert into a surging human traffic jam.

Catching an actual glimpse of him required strategy, speed and luck.

Spectators hurried across dusty paths and scrambled up rocky slopes, trying to get ahead of the enormous gallery following Woods. Those caught behind the ropes often saw little more than the top of his cap. By the time many reached a green, every patch of high ground was occupied and Woods had already struck his shot.

The scene felt less like a golf tournament than a traveling parade. Volunteers pleaded with fans to keep moving. Camera shutters snapped. Cheers rolled across the cactus-lined course whenever Woods appeared—or whenever the crowd assumed he had.

Yet beneath the excitement was the question that has followed Woods throughout his comeback: Will the repaired knee hold up?

The early signs were encouraging. His swing looked powerful, his stride purposeful. There was no obvious limp as he negotiated the undulating course, and he showed flashes of the control and competitive intensity that made his absence so conspicuous.

But one round cannot duplicate the strain of four consecutive days, let alone an entire season. Match play can be especially demanding here, with long walks over uneven desert terrain and the possibility of playing multiple rounds in a short span. Every awkward stance, hard pivot and steep climb offered another test.

Woods could answer questions about pain and rehabilitation. He could insist that the knee was strong. Only tournament golf, however, could deliver the verdict.

For the spectators racing from hole to hole, that uncertainty was part of the attraction. They had come not merely to watch a famous golfer hit shots, but to witness the first steps of a comeback—and to see whether the body carrying him could withstand the journey.

If they could see him at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

His opening shot showed little sign of rust: a powerful, controlled drive sent safely down the fairway. The instant it landed, the ropes seemed to release a human tide. Thousands of fans surged after him, scrambling down both sides of the hole in a dusty stampede as marshals struggled to maintain order.

Woods went on to win the match, but the larger story was the atmosphere he created simply by being there. The galleries were bigger, the noise louder and every swing felt consequential. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 500-word news feature in the voice of a CNN reporter who believes golf is a frustrating spectator sport, using Tiger Woods’s long-awaited return in Marana as the central example.
counterfactuals.output:
**MARANA, Arizona —** Golf asks a lot of its spectators: patience, sturdy shoes, tolerance for whispering and, occasionally, the ability to stare at an empty patch of desert while wondering where the world’s most famous athlete has gone.

Tiger Woods’ long-awaited return at the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship offered a perfect example.

After eight months away from competition following reconstructive surgery on his left knee, Woods arrived at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Club at Dove Mountain in February 2009 carrying the expectations of an entire sport. Television helicopters circled above the Sonoran Desert. Fans crowded against ropes before sunrise. Camera crews tracked his every step.

Then came the frustrating part: watching him play golf.

Unlike a stadium sport, golf provides no guarantee of a good view. Thousands of spectators followed Woods’ opening match against Australia’s Brendan Jones, but only those positioned several rows deep could glimpse much more than his cap, his shoulders or the arc of a club. Others hurried across dusty paths, guessing where he might appear next.

A roar in the distance often served as the first indication that Woods had done something memorable.

There is undeniable drama in that delayed reaction. News travels across a golf course like weather. One gallery cheers, another turns its head, and suddenly everyone knows Woods has made a putt — even if most did not see it.

But it is an odd way to consume a sporting comeback.

Woods provided an encouraging opening act, defeating Jones 3 and 2. His swing looked controlled, his repaired knee held up, and his familiar red-shirt intensity returned. For golf, which had spent months missing its biggest attraction, it felt like order had been restored.

Yet match play can be as abrupt as it is compelling. A day later, South Africa’s Tim Clark beat Woods 4 and 2, ending the comeback almost as soon as it began.

The result exposed another hazard for spectators. Fans had traveled to Arizona expecting several days of Tiger. Instead, one poor round sent him home. No consolation game. No weekend appearance. Just a retreat to the parking lot and a tournament forced to continue without the man many had come to see.

That does not mean golf lacks beauty. Dove Mountain’s broad desert views were spectacular, and the intimacy of hearing club strike ball can be thrilling. Match play, with one golfer directly confronting another, also offers a clarity often missing from sprawling stroke-play leaderboards.

Still, the Woods experience in Marana showed why golf can be maddening from outside the ropes. The sport’s central figure returned after months of uncertainty, and thousands gathered to witness history. Many witnessed backs, hats and raised camera phones instead.

Woods’ comeback was brief, significant and tantalizingly incomplete — which, for a golf spectator, felt entirely appropriate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

Include details about the range, first-hole crowds, obstructive TV crews, soaring heat, and concerns over his “bionic knee.”

**MARANA, Arizona —** Fans arrived at Dove Mountain hours before Tiger Woods’ opening-round tee time, staking out patches of desert and crowding around the practice range to witness the world No. 1’s first competitive appearance in more than eight months.

By the time Woods began warming up for his match against Australian Brendan Jones at the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship, spectators were packed several rows deep behind the range ropes. Every swing drew attention, with particular scrutiny reserved for the left knee he had reconstructed after winning the U.S. Open the previous June.

The crowd at the first hole was larger still. Grandstands filled early, while thousands lined the fairway in the rising Arizona heat. Some who had waited for hours complained that television crews, camera platforms and officials repeatedly blocked their view as Woods moved from the tee into the desert course.

Temperatures climbed sharply under a cloudless sky, testing spectators who had come prepared for a long day. Many nevertheless remained in place, eager for even a brief look at the player whose repaired joint had already been dubbed the “bionic knee.”

Woods showed little sign of discomfort. His stride appeared confident, his swing aggressive and his competitive instincts intact as he defeated Jones 3 and 2. The victory answered the first question about his comeback, but concerns over how the knee would withstand repeated rounds—and the demands of a full season—remained.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
